Abaye raises a second, similar baraita with baskets and containers, reaching the same conclusion.
Abaye explains that under Torah law the second baraita would be forbidden, so the ruling must rest on rabbinic law.

ranges.en: Abaye objects: on Rav Dimi's view the teruma case is still forbidden, since an olive-bulk of teruma is eaten regardless of proportion.
Rav Dimi replies: teruma in the present era applies only by rabbinic law, so the lenient ruling holds.
Abaye asks what shows that the verse teaches permitted combining, rather than that forbidden flavor takes the status of its substance.
Narrates Abaye's shift: he had objected to Rav Dimi, then proposed deriving from the verse that forbidden flavor has the status of its substance.
Abaye accepts Rav Dimi's answer and proposes the verse establishes that forbidden flavor is like its substance.
Baraita: soaked grapes in water that tastes of wine make a nazirite liable, as the flavor takes the status of wine.
From here one derives that all Torah prohibitions follow this rule.
Kal vachomer from the nazirite: his prohibition is temporary and permits some items, so flavor should count.
Vineyard kilayim are a permanent prohibition, so flavor should count there too; orlah is similar.
A sage asks R. Abahu which of R. Akiva's views is meant, and whether it is the case of the mishna.
Mishna: R. Akiva says even one who soaked bread in wine, with enough to combine to an olive-bulk, is liable.
Asks whether Akiva's ruling is about an olive-bulk being present instead.
Akiva's teaching is meant to exclude the first tanna's quarter-log view; the case is Akiva's own.
Baraita: Rabbi Akiva says a nazirite who soaked bread in wine and ate an olive-bulk of bread and wine is liable.
Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi how Rabbi Akiva's view is to be read in this case.
Asks how one derives that permitted combines with forbidden, rather than that flavor counts as substance.
Derives from meat cooked in milk: that is mere taste yet forbidden, so the same applies here.
The Sages do not learn from meat in milk, since it is a novelty.
Asks what the novelty of meat in milk is.
Objection: each item alone is permitted but together forbidden, as with kilayim, so the rule may concern combination instead.

ranges.en: Akiva derives from purging gentile vessels taken as spoil that flavor counts as substance, citing Numbers 31:23.

For gentile vessels the Torah forbids even tainting flavor, a novelty that Akiva accepts as well.

Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi whether the Sages' view implies the same ruling for Rabbi Akiva.
The Rabbis hold the verse teaches flavor like substance; from here all Torah prohibitions follow, and Akiva agrees.
Asks whether one derives all Torah prohibitions from this verse.
Reply: the nazirite and sin-offering are two verses written together, which cannot teach each other.
Asks what the sin-offering case is.
Leviticus 6:20: whatever touches its flesh becomes holy; the words in its flesh limit this to absorbed items.
Both verses are needed: a sin-offering verse alone would not extend to the nazirite, since nazirite items are not sacred.
Akiva asks what purpose the two verses serve.
Akiva replies that the verse should be written for the nazirite, so the sin-offering can be derived from it.
The Rabbis reply: the sin-offering teaches permitted combining, while non-sacred items are not derived from sacred ones.
Both Akiva and the Rabbis hold permitted combines with forbidden; two verses written together teach nothing.
Rav Ashi tells Rav Kahana: rather, consider the baraita on the nazirite's prohibitions from the vine.
Numbers 6:4: from anything made of the vine; this teaches that nazirite prohibitions combine with one another, per Akiva.
Asks whether permitted combines with forbidden, and whether forbidden combines with forbidden, requires further study.
Permitted combines with forbidden at once, and forbidden with forbidden even separately; Rabbi Shimon's view is introduced.

ranges.en: Asks what Rabbi Shimon derives from the grapevine verse, given he denies combination of permitted and forbidden

Rabbi Elazar's principle: permitted matter combines with forbidden only for the nazirite's quarter-log in the Torah
Asks what the difference is between Rabbi Yochanan's and Rabbi Elazar's formulations
Rabbi Yochanan extends the combination rule to include even foods, not only liquids
Rabbi Elazar limits combination to liquids; other foods do not combine
Rabbi Elazar says there are ten quarter-log applications, and Rav Kahana held a mnemonic
The mnemonic: five red items (nazirite, Paschal, instructing, Temple, death) and five white ones
The nazirite item: a quarter-log of wine for which a nazirite is liable
The Paschal item: Shmuel's ruling that the four cups must each contain a quarter-log
The instructing item: one who drank a quarter-log of wine may not instruct in the Temple, and entering is liable to death
A baraita derives from a verse that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses defiles in a tent
The five white items: challah, nazirite and leper oil, and leper water, disqualified on Shabbat
Cites a mishnah in Shabbat that liquids defile and disqualify at a quarter-log
Cites a second mishnah that liquids and effluents disqualify at a quarter-log
Objects that there is no other case, but there is a quarter-log for washing hands, for one or two people
The mishnah does not deal with that case, where the parties dispute it
Objects with a clay pot into which one puts half a log of water from the sink

Objects that one may put any amount of water into the pot
Rabbi Zakkai says the quarter-log refers to a disputed case, which the mishnah does not address
Objects that there is a mikveh, except for the one the Sages nullified

ranges.en: The mishnah: a nazirite is liable for eating grapes only when he eats an olive-bulk of them
Explains the first tanna: the other nazirite prohibitions are not compared to drinking, so drinking is measured by a quarter-log
Rabbi Akiva holds that the olive-bulk measure applies to liquids as well
Akiva derives from the verse on fresh and dried grapes that every nazirite prohibition is measured by an olive-bulk
The mishnah: he is liable separately for drinking wine, eating grapes, grape seeds and grape skins
A baraita: the verse makes each grape product a separate liability, and from it one derives the rule for all Torah prohibitions
Analogy: where one kind has two names, one is liable for each name separately, as with grapes
The principle includes new wine and grapes, which are distinct names for the same kind
Abaye: one who eats a seed or skin is flogged twice, and seed plus skin three times
Rava: one is flogged only once for a seed or skin, since a general prohibition is not a separate flogging
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye with a statement of Rabbi Eliezer
Rabbi Eliezer: a nazirite who drinks all day is liable once, but is flogged for each warning he ignores
Eliezer's list: eating grapes, raisins, seeds, skins and squeezing juice, for which he is flogged five times
If Abaye is right, he should be flogged six times, including the verse on anything made of the grapevine
Abaye responds that Rabbi Eliezer taught some prohibitions and omitted others
Asks what else Rabbi Eliezer omitted
He omitted the prohibition of not profaning one's word, which the nazirite violated by breaking his vow
If that is the reason, it is not an omission, since Eliezer lists only prohibitions unique to nazirites
Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that Eliezer also omitted the case of the substances in between seed and skin
Rav Pappa replies that Eliezer did not teach five sets of lashes, only that he is flogged for each action
The Gemara begins a further question: but

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why did Rav Pappa object to Abaye when the baraita does not teach five sets of lashes?
Rav Pappa thought Abaye's view was only his opinion, so he would retract it; he did not know it was a tradition
The mishnah: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya requires at least two seeds and one skin to form an olive-bulk
Asks in accordance with whose opinion the verse is translated as seeds and skins
The translation follows Rabbi Yosei's opinion
Mishnah: a nazirite who is shaved, even by bandits or by pulling a hair, must restart thirty days
Dilemma: does hair grow from the root or from the tip, and what practical difference does that make?
It matters for a nazirite shaved by bandits who left enough hair to bend its end to its root
If hair grows from the root, the vowed hair is gone and days must be added; if from the tip, some vowed hair remains
Come and hear: a live louse found at the root suggests the hair grows from the tip
Rejects the proof: a live louse descends with the hair while feeding, so growth from the root still fits
Come and hear: a dead louse found at the tip suggests the hair grows from the root
Rejects the proof: a dead louse has no strength and stays where it died as the hair grows
Come and hear: gentiles' braided hair is loose underneath, suggesting growth from the bottom
Rejects the proof: braided hair crumples where someone lies on it, so it looks loose underneath
Dyed sheep wool is loose underneath, and beards dyed by old men turn white, supporting growth from the bottom

ranges.en: The Gemara concludes that the dyed-wool proof shows hair grows from the bottom
Objects with a baraita: a nazirite shaved by bandits who keeps enough hair to bend to its root does not forfeit days, which contradicts growth from the bottom
The baraita refers to shaving after the term ends, and it is Rabbi Eliezer's view that this negates only seven days
Asks what the reason of Rabbi Eliezer is
He derives the shaving of purity from the shaving of impurity, which requires waiting seven days
The Sages accept that hair grows enough every seven days to bend its end to its root
The mishnah: a nazirite who shaves with a razor, scissors or by pulling, even a small amount, is liable
A baraita derives from the verses that any hair removal, including tearing and pulling, is forbidden, following Rabbi Yoshiya
Rabbi Yonatan: only a razor is forbidden, and tearing or pulling is exempt
Asks: but is it not written that he shall be holy?
Shaving with a razor violates both a positive commandment of holiness and a prohibition
Another baraita derives from the verse that he shall not pass a razor over his head that all removal is forbidden

The razor is not learned for the final shaving from the leper's case, so the verse must specify it for the purity shaving

ranges.en: A lenient halakha cannot be derived from a stricter one to make the lenient case stringent, so the leper case needs its own verse

Asks: but is it not written that a razor shall not pass over his head, which would conflict with that reading?
The phrase teaches that a razor use transgresses two prohibitions, one for removing hair and one for using a razor
Rav Hisda: one hair brings flogging, two hairs invalidate the purity shaving, and negating days requires most of the head, done only with a razor
Asks: if the verse includes all hair-removing implements, why restrict it, and how should Rav Hisda's view be read?
A baraita states that removing hair by any means negates days only if most of the head is shaved, in the manner of a razor
Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda: as two hairs prevent a valid shaving, two hairs also negate the days of the vow
Mishnah: nazirites, lepers and Levites must shave, and a shaving with another implement or leaving two hairs is invalid
Asks: why teach that the three shave as a mitzva, since that is obvious from the Torah
The mishnah is needed so one does not think the mitzva is only hair removal, which a depilatory would satisfy
Granted for nazirite and Levites, the verse is explicit, but how do we know the leper must shave with a razor?
Hypothetical derivation: as Levites must shave with a razor, so must lepers, since both must shave
Refutes the Levite analogy: Levites are waved on their bodies, which lepers are not, so the comparison fails
Derivation from both Levites and nazirites, whose offerings include bread, to the leper's shaving with a razor
The argument returns: the two cases are not comparable as a proof, since one is not like the other
Derives the leper's razor shaving from the shared feature of the Levites and nazirites: both require a shaving done with a razor
Rava asks Rav Ashi: let the shared feature be refuted, since one can object to it in the same way

ranges.en: Objects: the leper's offering includes a poverty option, unlike the nazirite and Levite offerings, so the analogy fails

Rava: that baraita follows the Rabbis, who derive the leper's shaving from the prohibition on destroying the beard
Cites a mishnah in Makkot: Rabbi Eliezer holds one is liable for beard-destruction with any implement, so he derives it by analogy
Asks what is the reason of the Rabbis for requiring a razor for the leper
A baraita: the verse's mention of the beard shows a leper who is a priest must still shave his beard
Asks from where we know the leper's shaving must be done with a razor
A baraita on the priest's beard prohibition: destruction means removing hairs entirely, which excludes scissors and tweezers
The destructive shaving is with a razor, so the implement forbidden to priests is the one required for the leper
Perhaps a leper who shaves with tweezers also fulfills the mitzva, and the verse only excludes liability for a razor

ranges.en: Objects: if shaving with tweezers is a mitzva, then the absence of the word razor should forbid a razor, per Reish Lakish

Asks what is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer for deriving that a leper must use a razor

It overrides the prohibition on rounding the corners of the head, as a baraita on the verse teaches

ranges.en: The fringes verse shows a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition, the general principle derived from the juxtaposition
Restates the mishnah's rule that shaving with another implement or leaving two hairs means they have done nothing
Rav Aha bar Rav Ika: the principle that a majority is like the whole applies by Torah law
Asks from where this principle is learned
The verse on a nazirite shaving on the seventh day shows that only a full removal fulfills the mitzva
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina objects: the verse concerns an impure nazirite, while the rule applies to a pure one too
Abaye asks: if a nazirite shaved, left two hairs, and later shaved them after regrowth, do they invalidate his shaving?

The difference is soil that does not scrape; the question remains unresolved
Mishnah: a nazirite who drinks wine all day is liable only once, but liable for each warned act of drinking
Mishnah: a nazirite who shaves all day is liable once, but liable for each warned act of shaving
Mishnah: a nazirite who becomes impure to the dead all day is liable once, but liable for each warned act of defilement

ranges.en: Rabba, citing Rav Huna: the verse on a nazirite and corpses warns against each contact and against entering, but not against a second contact

Rav Huna's case: a nazirite standing in a cemetery who is touched by another corpse is liable, so a second impurity counts
Abaye objects with a baraita: a priest already impure who is touched by a second corpse is not liable, so Rav Yosef's view fails
Rav Yosef responds: the mishnah then poses the same difficulty to you, since the nazirite is liable for each warned contact
The sources do not conflict: the baraita concerns concurrent contact, the mishnah contact after separation
Asks whether the concurrent impurity exemption applies by Torah law, given Rabbi Yannai's limitation to teruma and sacrifices
Two kinds of concurrent impurity: person-to-person contact is rabbinic, while contact with a corpse is Torah-level, so the second contact is not liable

ranges.en: Why should one who enters a house be liable twice, since the hand enters first and makes him impure before the rest of him enters

Objects: the nose must enter first, so impurity reaches him before the rest of the body enters, making the answer impossible
Rava: entering with a hand gives impurity alone; entering upright makes both occur together, since the head does not enter first
Objects: the toes must enter first, so impurity descends before the body enters, again making the answer impossible
Rav Pappa: the case is one who enters a chest or cabinet and another opens its cover over him, so both occur together
Mar bar Rav Ashi: the case is one who enters a house where a dying person's soul departs while he sits, so both occur together
A baraita: a priest is impure only once the person dies; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives the same from the nazirite verse on when they die
Asks what the difference is between these two derivations
Rabbi Yochanan: the difference lies in the interpretation of the verse, not in any practical halakha
Reish Lakish: the difference concerns a dying person, who imparts no impurity on the view derived from when they die

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: when they die excludes impurity from death itself, but leprosy and discharge still impart impurity to a nazirite
If the verse teaches a time of impurity, how does it also teach two halakhot from the same words
The verse should say when he dies; the emphasis on when they die teaches two halakhot, one for timing and one for corpse impurity only
The reverse question: if the verse on when they die teaches timing, why is the word to profane needed
To profane is needed to exclude a priest who is already profaned, so the prohibition applies only before the death
The same question in reverse: the word to profane would then be needed for this reasoning
If so, the verse should read to profane, and the word when they die then teaches two halakhot
Objects with a baraita: one is impure only when the soul departs, so the baraita distinguishes impurity from the start of the mourning restriction

ranges.en: Rav Chisda, citing Rav: a priest may not become impure to bury a father whose head was severed

Since the priest was walking on the road, he is considered as one who has no one to bury the father

Asks what it means that he may search for a barley-grain bone, since that would mean he defiles for a father missing a bit

The verse adds a different form of impurity, teaching that a priest may defile for a spine, skull and other bone counts

ranges.en: One might think a priest may not defile for a spine or skull of other relatives, but the sister's case shows he may, which challenges Rav
That baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav's ruling follows this same anonymous tanna
The story of Rabbi Yitzchak's father: after three years the body was not whole, so the priest could no longer defile to bury him
Mishnah: a nazirite is forbidden impurity, shaving and wine products; impurity and shaving negate his term, but wine does not
Mishnah continues: wine products are stricter than impurity and shaving in that they are never permitted, while impurity and shaving are permitted in cases of mitzva

The verse on the earlier days falling when his nazirite term was made impure shows impurity negates everything

The verse on the earlier days shows impurity negates everything, while a shaving negates only thirty days

The verse on impurity of the head of his vow shows shaving is not counted as impurity, so it cannot negate everything

The verse on the razor shows the prohibition applies to one who shaves, and a fortiori from wine shaving is not permitted in general
The verse on the head and beard shows the shaving is not permitted, and a fortiori from wine its negation is limited
Objects: a fortiori from shaving, wine should negate thirty days, but a fortiori fails because hair growth is required
Wine should negate thirty days a fortiori from shaving, since shaving is permitted and negates; wine should negate for the same reason

ranges.en: Mishnah: a nazirite made impure is sprinkled on days three and seven, shaves on day seven, and brings offerings on day eight, per Rabbi Akiva

ranges.en: Asks where the Gate of Nicanor stood, given that the impure and those lacking atonement stand there

ranges.en: Infers from the mishnah's wording that the witness was too far away to know which nazirite was impure, so both shave.
Asks why they may shave at all, since one may be pure and then shaving would violate the prohibition on rounding the head.
Shmuel answers: the case is a woman or a minor, who are not prohibited from rounding the head.
Objects that Shmuel could have read an adult male, so his choice implies he holds that rounding the whole head counts as rounding.
Mar Zutra applies Shmuel's ruling to the mishnah's latter clause about a nazirite of uncertain impurity.
Mishnah clause: a nazirite of uncertain impurity and uncertain leprosy eats sacred food after sixty days and shaves four times.
Raises the problem that the mishnah's nazirite rounds his head, though Shmuel limited this to a woman or minor.
Rav Huna rules that an adult who rounds a minor's head is liable.
Adda bar Ahava objects: who shaves Rav Huna's sons, since he rules an adult may not round a minor's head?
Rav Huna replies that Hova, his wife, does it, since she is not prohibited.
Rav Adda angrily curses that Hova should bury her sons for doing this.
The Gemara reports the curse took effect: Rav Huna's children died during Rav Adda's lifetime.
Asks what Rav Huna and Rav Adda disagree about, since both hold that rounding the whole head counts as rounding.

ranges.en: Baraita: the verse's his head overrides the rounding prohibition for lepers, and similarly a nazirite-leper must shave.

Rava rebuts: all agree whole-head shaving is not rounding; the verse addresses a leper who rounds corners then shaves the rest, which is exempt.
Objects: the verse cannot permit a prohibition ab initio, and Reish Lakish holds that a clashing mitzva overrides only if both cannot be fulfilled.
Rather, everyone agrees rounding the whole head is called rounding.
Asks where the rule that a mitzva overrides only a prohibition comes from, on the reading that the verse overrides both.
Answers that the fringes verse, read with the diverse-kinds prohibition, shows a mitzva overrides a prohibition.
Asks why the tanna derives the rule from his head instead of from the fringes verse.
Replies that the fringes verse was meant for Rava's case, so it does not teach the principle.
Rava raises a contradiction: the fringe must match the garment, yet diverse kinds of wool and linen are forbidden together.
Resolves it: wool-linen fringes exempt any garment, while other fringes exempt only garments of their own kind.
Asks how this tanna, who limits his head to a prohibition, knows a leper's shave overrides a nazirite's mitzva.
Answers that he derives it from the phrase his beard in Leviticus 14:9.
Baraita: his beard teaches that even a leper-priest, normally barred from shaving his beard, must shave.
Asks why the one who derives the principle from his head does not derive it from his beard instead.
Counters that on that reasoning, the beard verse would establish the general principle that a mitzva overrides a prohibition, as we hold generally.

ranges.en: Asks why the priest case cannot simply teach that a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition and another positive mitzva

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehoshua says the surviving nazirite should have a non-nazirite in the marketplace vow to correspond to him

Ben Zoma objects: who would agree to vow to be a nazirite corresponding to another, so the procedure cannot work

ranges.en: A tanna teaches that the thirty-day rule applies to a short naziriteship, while a year-long one requires two years before sacrificial food

Asks why the first shaving brings the two leper birds along with a sin-offering and a burnt-offering
Whichever case applies, the offerings are proper: leper birds for leprosy, a sin-offering for doubt, a burnt-offering as a gift
He cannot be shaved within seven days, because he may be only a nazirite, and the verse keeps the razor off until naziriteship ends
If he is impure but not a leper, the birds are performed outside the Temple and the burnt-offering counts as a gift
If he is neither leper nor impure, the offerings are still correct, and the burnt-offering fulfills his nazirite obligation

ranges.en: Concludes the analysis of the baraita: for a pure nazirite the first burnt-offering counts as obligation, and the later one as a gift, and reverse for impure
Case of a nazirite uncertain about impurity but a confirmed leper: eats sacrificial food after eight days and drinks wine after sixty-seven days
Case of an uncertain leper who is definitely impure: eats sacrificial food after thirty-seven days and drinks wine after seventy-four days
Case of a definitely impure, definitely leprous nazirite: eats sacrificial food after eight days and drinks wine after forty-four days
Students ask Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai whether one shaving can count for both a pure nazirite and a leper
Rabbi Shimon replies that one shaving cannot serve both requirements

The two shavings have different aims: a nazirite shaves to remove hair, while a leper shaves to let hair grow

Students propose that the shaving could count for leprosy and for the impure nazirite shaving, both before the sprinkling
An impure nazirite shaves after immersion in water, while a leper shaves before immersion, so they still differ
The students concede that one shaving should not count for both the days of counting and the naziriteship
Asks why it should not at least count for leprosy and impure naziriteship, since both shavings aim to grow hair

ranges.en: Rabbi Hiyya teaches that a leper's shaving does not count toward a nazirite's shaving, since the timing relative to immersion and blood differs
Quotes the mishna's rule that the shaving of leprosy is the stated case of overriding
Rami bar Hama asks whether the four shavings are for a mitzva or for removing impure hair

Asks what the halakha is, and Rava offers a resolution

Closing formula marking the end of the chapter Two Nazirites
Mishna: gentiles have no naziriteship, while women and slaves may take it, with a husband unable to annul his wife's vow
The mishna teaches that gentiles have no naziriteship while women and Canaanite slaves do

ranges.en: Mishna: a slave's vows are a greater stringency, since a husband can nullify his wife's vows but not his slave's, and the slave completes naziriteship when freed

ranges.en: Mishna: a nazirite who learns of a known impurity during his naziriteship negates it, while an unknown deep-grave impurity does not

Mishna: a zav is examined in seven ways before confirmed as a zav; after confirmation, all discharges are impure, including semen
Baraita: one who strikes another and is later judged to have died from the blow is liable, while Rabbi Nehemya exempts him
Asks from where these rules about examining a zav before and not after confirmation are derived
Rabbi Natan: the verse zav et zovo, read as a male like a female, shows no examination after two discharges
But Rabbi Eliezer teaches that a third discharge is examined and a fourth is not, which conflicts with this verse
The tanna Rabbi Eliezer expounds instances of the word et, while the Rabbis do not, so the verse alludes to two discharges only
Mishna: the discharge caused by circumstances beyond control, and the uncertain one, are considered impure

ranges.en: Rava: the uncertainty is not whether he saw a discharge but its cause, and a zav's uncertain case is impure; the mishna says his semen is impure
Asks what halakha the mishna teaches about the semen of a zav, since contact impurity is no stricter than that of a pure man
Rather, the semen of a zav renders people impure even by carrying, like the impurity of ziva
Asks who taught that a zav's semen imparts impurity by carrying
Objects that the baraita's Rabbi Yehoshua only meant the droplets of ziva mixed in, so the source does not prove the semen itself transmits by carrying
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the mishna means one does not attribute a discharge to the semen, so later discharges count as ziva
Rav Pappa proposes that since the zav is weakened by prior ziva, any later discharge is ziva even after emission
Rava objects from the mishna on a convert, who becomes a zav immediately without any prior weakness
Rav Pappa replies that accepting the mitzvot is itself a greater illness, so the convert case is the same
Rather, the dispute over carrying is between tanna'im: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua hold it imparts by carrying, while Rabbi Yosei limits it to that day
Asks what the basis of the dispute between the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei is
The dispute is over Shmuel's contradiction between the verses about a man who is not pure by night and bathes at evening
One who reads from evening to evening infers two evenings, while the other reads night as limiting it to that same day
Asks how the view that the evening verse means two evenings deals with the verse about night
The night verse is no proof, since it describes the usual case, when seminal emission happens at night
Mishna: Samuel was a nazirite, following Rabbi Nehorai, because the word mora is used of Samson and of Samuel
Just as mora used of Samson means naziriteship, so mora used of Samuel also means naziriteship
Rabbi Yosei objects that mora means only the fear of flesh and blood, so it should be read with an alef
Rabbi Nehorai replies that Samuel's own words show he feared Saul, so mora must mean a razor and Samuel was a nazirite
Gemara opens with Rav speaking to his son Hiyya

ranges.en: Rav Huna instructs his son Rabba to seize the chance to recite the blessing over the cup.
The Gemara asks whether reciting a blessing is preferable to answering amen, given a baraita saying the opposite.
Rabbi Nehorai confirms the baraita and illustrates it with the image of the military assistants leading the battle.
The Gemara resolves the conflict: it is a dispute between tanna'im.
The baraita itself: both the reciter and the responder are included in the verse, but the reciter is rewarded first.
Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Hanina, teaches that Torah scholars increase peace in the world.
Isaiah 54:13 is cited, read homiletically as builders rather than children, to support that teaching.
Closing formula ending the chapter and tractate, noting that the Samaritans cannot take Nazirite vows.
